lines.text: Investigators, journalists and lawyers share one problem: too much evidence to read, and a result nobody can later prove was not changed.
Sealbook works in three steps.
You bring the material in.
The app reads all of it and proposes connections, each with the exact place it came from.
A person approves or declines each one with a signature, and the record is sealed, so anyone can check it later.
Four invented cases show how that helps.
One: a freight company pays a supplier, a consultant, a guarantor and a ship agent. Four desks, four clean files.
Are they four people, or one man under four names? The desks hold 14 sources and 1,445 rows.
lines.say: Are they four people, or one man under four names? The desks hold fourteen sources and one thousand, four hundred and forty-five rows.

lines.text: Kassar. Qassar. Khassar. Kasar. And on one licence, the name in Arabic.
Four spellings, two alphabets, one man. And one who is not him: a surveyor with the same name, born elsewhere.
The app proposed each link with the passage behind it. Fixed rules, with no AI model, found 6 of the 6 true links, and offered the surveyor too.
lines.say: The app proposed each link with the passage behind it. Fixed rules, with no AI model, found six of the six true links, and offered the surveyor too.

lines.text: A person declines the surveyor, with a reason, and signs each decision with a passkey on their own device.
The case closes on a conclusion, signed by a person and checked by a colleague: one man, under four names.
Two: a workshop burns down at night. The bookkeeper says she spent the evening at her sister's, 34 kilometres away.
lines.say: Two: a workshop burns down at night. The bookkeeper says she spent the evening at her sister's, thirty-four kilometres away.

lines.text: Was she? There are 41 statements to read.
lines.say: Was she? There are forty-one statements to read.

lines.text: The app reads every paper itself. On this scanned exhibit sheet, it reads the page, then pulls out who was where, boxed where it is written.
It describes the photograph from her phone, and writes down the voice note she sent.
Then it flags what does not fit: those two exhibits place her at the workshop at 21:52 and 22:07, while she says she was away from six.
lines.say: Then it flags what does not fit: those two exhibits place her at the workshop at twenty-one fifty-two and twenty-two oh seven, while she says she was away from six.

lines.text: A person checks both against her statement and signs: she was at the yard on Tanner's Row that evening, not in Brindle Cross from six.
Three: a flood video spreads as breaking news.
Is it new? The tip line holds 36 clips that look alike.
lines.say: Is it new? The tip line holds thirty-six clips that look alike.

lines.text: The app compares their sound and ties the viral clip to a video posted two years earlier. It had been cropped and mirrored, so the picture no longer matched.
8 of 9 reposts were tied this way; one muted copy is missed. A person signs that the clip is old.
lines.say: Eight of nine reposts were tied this way; one muted copy is missed. A person signs that the clip is old.

lines.text: Four: a nurse boards a night bus and is never seen again.
Where do you look? The bus company's logs run to several hundred lines.
A supervisor's statement says when the driver was last seen. From that night, the app finds 73 days in which no log names him.
lines.say: A supervisor's statement says when the driver was last seen. From that night, the app finds seventy-three days in which no log names him.

lines.text: The conclusion, signed and checked by a colleague: Aron Vesk is named in no log for the next 73 days; this is a lead to follow, not a finding about what he did.
lines.say: The conclusion, signed and checked by a colleague: Aron Vesk is named in no log for the next seventy-three days; this is a lead to follow, not a finding about what he did.

lines.text: Every decision is signed by a person, and the case is sealed. Here the first case's real package is checked in a browser, with nothing uploaded.
The machine reads more than a person can, and finds the links. A person approves every one.
